notes.claim: A drive has three parts: a rectifier turns AC to DC, a DC bus with capacitors smooths it, and an inverter switches it back to AC at chosen frequency and voltage by pulse-width modulation.
Motor speed follows the supply frequency, so a drive that sets the frequency sets the speed.
Voltage is lowered in proportion to frequency so the flux stays constant (constant V/f); otherwise the motor draws excessive current at low frequency, with saturation.

Below the nominal frequency is the constant flux range; above it the voltage can rise no further and the motor is in field weakening, where it can run at constant power, so maximum torque falls with frequency.
A drive's soft start removes the inrush of a direct start and the mechanical shock.
For fans and pumps power varies roughly as the cube of speed: half speed needs about one eighth power in theory; a maker says treat the savings as theoretical.
Slowing a conveyor from 100% to 80% saves 20% of energy while a pump or fan saves nearer 50%, so savings are large only on variable-torque loads.
VFDs on ships are used on cranes, winches, bow thrusters, ventilation, pumps and compressors (a maker's list).
Fast-rising voltage pulses and high switching frequencies of modern drives can send current pulses through motor bearings that erode the races.
A drive trip on over-voltage during stopping can come from regenerated energy: the fix named is a longer deceleration time or a brake chopper; harmonics can also overcharge the DC link capacitors.
Earth-fault trips are found from the sum of the output currents and often from weak or damp insulation; disconnect the drive before an insulation resistance test on the motor and cable.
